pdm-transfusion: What causes most fatal hemolytic transfusion reactions?
Clerical error at the bedside, not laboratory testing
Where is a pre-transfusion sample labeled?
At the bedside, in front of the patient
Against what are the patient and unit details matched at the bedside?
The patient's wristband
How are the first 25 to 50 mL of a transfusion given?
Slowly (critical first 15 minutes)
As little as how much incompatible blood can cause a severe acute hemolytic reaction?
25 mL
What is required when there is no prior verified blood type on record?
A second, separate sample to confirm ABO/Rh
What does a group O red cell carry?
Only the unmodified H antigen
Which enzyme does group A possess?
N-acetylgalactosamine transferase
Which enzyme does group B possess?
D-galactosyltransferase
What primes the naturally occurring ABO antibodies?
Gut flora and food carbohydrates in infancy
Which antibody class are the ABO antibodies?
IgM (pentamer, fixes complement)
Where are red cells destroyed in an ABO mismatch?
In the circulation (intravascular, membrane attack complex)
Which complement products cause the hypotension of an ABO reaction?
The anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a
What injures the kidney in an ABO reaction?
Free hemoglobin (tubular precipitation, acute tubular necrosis)
Which plasma antibody does group A have?
Anti-B
Universal red cell donor?
Group O
Universal red cell recipient?
Group AB
Universal plasma donor?
Group AB
Universal plasma recipient?
Group O
Group B can receive red cells from?
B or O
Group A can receive plasma from?
A or AB
Emergency red cells for a woman under 50 of unknown type?
O-negative
Emergency red cells for an adult man of unknown type?
O-positive
Does an Rh-negative man given O-positive cells hemolyze immediately?
No; he may form anti-D later
What does Rh-positive mean?
The RhD polypeptide is present on the red cell
What kind of molecule is RhD?
A transmembrane protein
Most immunogenic red cell antigen outside ABO?
RhD
How much anti-D does an unexposed Rh-negative person have?
None
Which antibody class is anti-D?
IgG (mainly IgG1 and IgG3)
Where are anti-D-coated cells destroyed?
Splenic macrophages (extravascular)
How does anti-D reach the fetus?
IgG crosses the placenta via Fc receptors
What is the end stage of severe fetal hemolysis from anti-D?
Hydrops fetalis (high-output heart failure)
When is routine Rh immune globulin given in pregnancy?
At about 28 weeks
Post-partum Rh immune globulin window?
Within 72 hours of delivering an RhD-positive baby
Name three events after which Rh immune globulin must be given.
Miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, abortion, amniocentesis, abdominal trauma (any three)
Which test quantifies a fetal-maternal hemorrhage?
Kleihauer-Betke test
How does Rh immune globulin work?
It masks and clears fetal D-positive cells before maternal B cells respond
What does forward typing detect?
Antigens on the patient's red cells
What does reverse typing detect?
Antibodies in the patient's plasma
Reverse typing: only A1 cells agglutinate. Group?
Group B
Reverse typing: only B cells agglutinate. Group?
Group A
Reverse typing: neither cell agglutinates. Group?
Group AB
Forward typing: no reaction with anti-A or anti-B. Group?
Group O
Forward and reverse types disagree. What happens?
No blood released; immediate investigation
What does the antibody screen find?
Unexpected IgG alloantibodies to non-ABO antigens
Which reagent cells does the antibody screen use?
2 to 3 group O reagent cells
Next step after a positive antibody screen?
An 11- to 16-cell identification panel
Why order a type and screen early before elective surgery?
Antigen-negative units can take hours or days to find
Electronic crossmatch requirement?
Negative screen AND two concordant type records
Immediate-spin crossmatch requirement?
Negative screen, no history of significant antibodies
Full antiglobulin crossmatch requirement?
Positive screen or history of significant antibodies
Purpose of the immediate-spin crossmatch?
Final ABO check; rules out a clerical mismatch
Slowest crossmatch tier?
Full antiglobulin (45 to 60+ minutes per unit)
Direct antiglobulin test specimen?
The patient's washed red cells (in vivo coating)
Indirect antiglobulin test uses?
Antibody screen, prenatal screen, crossmatching
Positive polyspecific direct test: next?
Retest with monospecific anti-IgG and anti-C3d
Type and screen: units held?
Zero
Type and crossmatch: units held?
Specific units tagged and reserved
When is a sample valid for only 72 hours?
Transfused or pregnant within 3 months, or uncertain history
First step for any suspected transfusion reaction?
Stop the transfusion (do not just slow it)
How is the line kept open after stopping?
Fresh saline through new tubing; never flush the old line
What happens to the bag and tubing after a reaction?
Returned to the blood bank for testing and cultures
Acute hemolytic reaction triad?
Fever and rigors, flank pain, red urine
Acute hemolytic: haptoglobin and LDH (lactate dehydrogenase)?
Undetectable haptoglobin, markedly high LDH
Why can the direct test be negative in an acute hemolytic reaction?
All donor cells were instantly lysed
Acute hemolytic renal labs?
Rising urea nitrogen and creatinine; hyperkalemia
Onset of a delayed hemolytic reaction?
3 to 30 days (peak 5 to 15)
Why did the screen miss a delayed hemolytic reaction?
The old antibody had fallen below detection
Smear finding in a delayed hemolytic reaction?
Spherocytes
Sickle cell clue to a delayed hemolytic reaction?
Hemoglobin A falls disproportionately
Hyperhemolysis syndrome?
Donor AND own cells destroyed; more transfusion can be fatal
Febrile non-hemolytic: temperature definition?
Rise of at least 1 °C to at least 38 °C, during or within 4 hours
Febrile non-hemolytic: labs?
All normal (negative direct antiglobulin test, clear plasma and urine)
Febrile reaction: when to work up sepsis?
Fever 2 °C or more, hypotension, or platelets
Prevents febrile non-hemolytic reactions?
Pre-storage leukoreduction
Allergic reaction mechanism?
Recipient IgE against donor plasma proteins
Allergic reactions are most frequent with?
Plasma-rich products (fresh frozen plasma, platelets)
Which reaction can restart the same unit?
Allergic, skin-only and fully resolved (slower, within 4-hour hang time)
Classic cause of transfusion anaphylaxis?
Severe IgA deficiency with anti-IgA
Anaphylaxis onset?
Seconds to minutes, after only 1 to 5 mL
Separates anaphylaxis from acute hemolysis and sepsis?
No fever
First-line drug for transfusion anaphylaxis?
Intramuscular epinephrine
Anaphylaxis lab test, and its window?
Serum tryptase within 1 to 3 hours
Future transfusions after anti-IgA anaphylaxis?
Washed red cells or IgA-deficient donors
Which reactions have a newly positive direct test?
Acute and delayed hemolytic
